questions.prompt:
note.txt said 'draft two' when you ran `git add`, and you then changed it to 'draft three'. You now run `git commit -m "Revise note"`. What does the new commit hold for note.txt?

Starting commands:
echo draft one > note.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Start note"
echo draft two > note.txt
git add note.txt
echo draft three > note.txt

Then run:
git commit -m "Revise note"
choices: draft three
draft two
draft one
Nothing: the commit is refused because the file changed
questions.explanation: Right: `git add` copied draft two into the staging area, and commit freezes the staging area.

questions.prompt: `git diff` prints nothing, but `git diff --cached` shows a change to map.txt. What will `git commit -m "Update map"` do?
choices: Commit the map.txt change; working tree, staging area and the new commit then all agree
Refuse, because the working tree has no changes
Commit nothing, because diff was empty
Commit map.txt and also any untracked files
questions.explanation: Right: empty `git diff` means working tree = staging area; the cached diff is exactly what the commit adds.

questions.prompt:
You are on main and you have edited map.txt but not committed. lighthouse points at the same commit as main. What happens in this lab when you run `git switch lighthouse`?

Starting commands:
echo coastline > map.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Start the map"
git branch lighthouse
echo coastline and reefs > map.txt

Then run:
git switch lighthouse
choices: It switches and your edit is lost
It refuses and changes nothing, so you can commit or undo first
It switches and commits your edit to lighthouse
It switches and your edit comes along
questions.explanation: Right for this lab: any uncommitted tracked change blocks the switch, and nothing changes. Real Git would carry this edit along, because both branches hold the same map.txt (see Real Git). It refuses only when the edit would be overwritten.

questions.prompt: main and docs both point at c4. You are on docs and commit c5. Then you run `git switch -c fix`. Where does fix point?
choices: c4, because branches start where main is
c5, the commit you are on
Nowhere until you commit on it
c4, because new branches start at the first commit
questions.explanation: Right: you were on docs at c5, so fix starts at c5 and includes that commit.

questions.prompt:
From the common ancestor (price 4), main changed price.txt to 5 and sale changed it to 3. On main you run `git merge sale`. What happens in this lab?

Starting commands:
echo price 4 > price.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Set price"
git switch -c sale
echo price 3 > price.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Sale price"
git switch main
echo price 5 > price.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Raise price"

Then run:
git merge sale
choices: main gets price 3 (the branch you merge in wins)
main keeps price 5 (your branch wins)
The merge refuses with a conflict and nothing changes
Git averages them to price 4
questions.explanation: Right: same file, two different changes from the ancestor. You must decide the final text. Real Git also stops here, writes conflict markers into price.txt and waits for you.

questions.prompt: feature has 2 new commits and main has 0 new commits since feature started. On main you run `git merge feature`. How many new commits does the merge create?
choices: 0, it's a fast-forward
1 merge commit
2 copies of feature's commits
It refuses until main has a commit
questions.explanation: Right: main's label just moves to feature's tip.

questions.prompt:
topic's commit is c2 (parent c1). main moved to c3. On topic you run `git rebase main`. Afterwards, which commit does topic point at?

Starting commands:
echo a > a.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m Base
git switch -c topic
echo b > b.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Topic work"
git switch main
echo c > c.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Main work"
git switch topic

Then run:
git rebase main
choices: c2, edited so its parent is c3
A new commit c4 whose parent is c3; c2 still exists, unpointed
A merge commit with parents c2 and c3
c3, and c2's change is dropped
questions.explanation: Right: rebase copies. The original c2 is left behind with no label.

questions.prompt: Your teammate opened a pull request from branch shared-fix, and two others have committed on top of it. main moved. Which is the safer way to bring main's changes into shared-fix?
choices: `git merge main` on shared-fix
`git rebase main` on shared-fix
Delete shared-fix and start again
Copy main's files in by hand
questions.explanation: Right: merge adds a commit and rewrites nothing others have built on.

questions.prompt:
notes.txt was never added. You run `git reset --hard HEAD~1`. What happens to code.txt and notes.txt?

Starting commands:
echo v1 > code.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version"
echo v2 > code.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Second version"
echo my ideas > notes.txt

Then run:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
choices: code.txt goes back to v1; notes.txt is deleted
code.txt goes back to v1; notes.txt is left alone
Both are left alone; only the branch moves
The reset refuses because notes.txt is untracked
questions.explanation: Right: tracked files match the target, untracked files survive.

questions.prompt: Your last commit had the right files but a bad message. Which reset lets you commit the exact same changes again with a new message in one command after it?
choices: git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
No reset can help
questions.explanation: Right: the changes stay staged, so `git commit -m "better"` recreates the commit.

questions.prompt:
You rebased topic (its old commit was c2; the copy is c4) and regret it. Which command puts topic back exactly as it was before the rebase?

Starting commands:
echo a > a.txt
git init
git add .
git commit -m Base
git switch -c topic
echo b > b.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Topic work"
git switch main
echo c > c.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Main work"
git switch topic
git rebase main

Then run:
git reset --hard c2
choices: git reset --hard HEAD~1
git reset --hard c2
git merge main
Nothing can: the rebase replaced c2
questions.explanation: Right: c2 is still in the graph, and resetting topic onto it restores the pre-rebase branch exactly.

questions.prompt: Which of these can you recover with Git alone?
choices: A commit your branch no longer points at after `reset --hard`
Edits you never staged, discarded by `reset --hard`
A file you created and never added, then deleted with rm
Text you typed and never saved to the file
questions.explanation: Right: it's a commit, so it still exists unreachable; find its id and reset or branch to it.
